doc.title: Catherine Russell interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 26, 2018

title: Women instrumentalists then and now
summary: Women were expected to sing or play piano, not horns; she discusses how that has and has not changed in 2018.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah. You know the thing about that is also that women were only supposed to play violin and piano and sing. They weren’t supposed to play the horn. Men didn’t want to see a horn in a woman’s mouth type of thing. So if you — or a bass, or something that was not considered a feminine type of a thing. So trumpet players and saxophone players, trombone players, you had to be strong enough to take all the criticism that went along

with that, from men and from other women. Why would you be playing that, you know what I mean? So some women lasted longer than others. Some lasted a few months or a year or something and then decided eh, I don’t want to do this, I want to have babies, I want to get married, I don’t want to do this anymore. And some had their families and continued to work as musicians. But still, when the war ended and the men came home a lot of them lost their gigs anyway, so it was like go back in the kitchen you know, where you belong.
Now that was over 70 years ago. Do you think the women in jazz in 2018 has changed that much?

Because women, in America at least, I mean we have a choice about what we want to do with out lives, and we’re not made to feel incomplete or anything like that you know what I mean, if we choose to continue to work instead of having children or whatever you know what I mean? So many of my female colleagues don’t — chose to work and to keep working and not take twenty years off to raise children. Because it’s one or the other in a lot of cases you know. So yeah, so I think that women are more respected as equals, as good musicians these days. But then, a lot of men still would prefer to work with other men. So I think it’s both.
